title: openai/openai-agents-python v0.24.0-alpha.8 — Agents SDK v0.24.0-alpha.8
body:
# Agents SDK v0.24.0-alpha.8

## Highlights

- **Approve Python tool calls before they run.** Review the arguments and approve or reject the call. You can remember a decision for the rest of the Session. [Managed approval example](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/managed_approvals/README.md#inspect-and-decide)
- **Connect your own model client.** The native tool loop works with async Responses and Chat Completions clients, LiteLLM, AnyLLM, and custom adapters. [Application-owned model clients](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/models.md#use-an-application-owned-model-client)
- **Add Realtime voice to a Session.** Use a server WebSocket, connect a browser over WebRTC, or attach to an existing SIP call. [Realtime connection options](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/native_voice.md#choose-a-connection)
- **Resume more kinds of work.** Save supported pending tool requests and approvals. Request and token budgets keep the usage already spent when you restore a supported checkpoint. [Restore a checkpoint with a budget](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/budgeted-recovery.md)
- **Install on more Linux systems.** The preview adds an ARM64 wheel. Both Linux wheels support glibc 2.28 or newer. [Preview wheel platform requirements](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/.github/RELEASING.md#L44)

## Added

- Observe tool-search calls, tool-search results, and hosted MCP approval decisions through `ModelOutputItemCompleted`. Use `include_execution_details=True` to receive full items; receive summaries by default. [Live tool observations](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/packages/codex/src/_agents_codex/observation.py#L238-L267)
- Use native Session Realtime APIs from `agents.realtime.native`, including `RealtimeAgentConfig(is_tool_enabled=...)`. Keep retained Classic/v0 Realtime imports under `agents.realtime`. [Native voice](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/native_voice.md#choose-a-connection) · [Classic imports](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/CLASSIC.md#compatible-voice-and-realtime-imports)
- Handle managed function approvals with `FunctionToolApprovalRequest` and `FunctionToolApprovalDecision`. Set `run_input_policy_before_approval=True` to run the input policy before the approval predicate as well as before execution. Return `FinishTurn(output)` from `tool_batch_completion` to propose a final value with output validation and completion checks. [Managed approvals](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c9

title: agno-agi/agno v3.2.0 — v3.2.0
body:
## Summary

Agno v3.2 makes Super Agent faster and more capable with direct tools, expands Company task governance and coordination, introduces database-backed AgentOS homepage metrics, upgrades A2A to the v1.0 protocol, updates the Slack interface to use the Bolt SDK and makes external agents first-class stored components.

## Changelog

## Breaking changes

- **OS Manager defaults and validation:** `OSManager.tool_call_limit` now defaults to 24 (was 8), and `num_history_runs` defaults to 5 (was 7). AgentOS refuses startup when `OSManager(root=...)` is combined with custom tools named `read_file`, `list_files`, or `search_content`.
- **A2A v1.0:** AgentOS and `A2AClient` now run on the official `a2a-sdk` 1.x, so upgrade the Agno server and client together. ([#10956](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/pull/10956))
    - The `/v1/message:*` and `/v1/tasks:*` routes are removed; use each entity's A2A endpoint instead.
    - Stream events and response artifacts follow the v1.0 shape.
    - The `a2a` extra now requires `a2a-sdk[http-server]>=1.2.2,<2`.
    - Direct imports of removed A2A helpers need updating.
    - Standard v0.3 clients still work through the compatibility wire by default.
- **Slack interface:** the interface now runs on Slack Bolt, and only the person who started a run can Approve or Deny it, unless they're named in `approvers=` or mapped to the same user with `users=`. ([#11599](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/pull/11599))
    - The `slack` extra now requires `slack_bolt>=1.29.0,<2` and `slack_sdk>=3.43.0,<4`; run `pip install -U "agno[slack]"`.
    - List anyone else who approves runs in `approvers=`.
    - AgentOS refuses startup when Slack serves `agent_os.manager` under `AgentOS(authorization=...)` or an authorization middleware without `users=`.
    - Direct imports of removed internal Slack helpers (`SlackEventHandler`, `HITLHandler`, `verify_slack_signature`) need updating.

## New features

- **Super Agent:** Super Agent now does the work itself instead of routing requests through manager members. Platform Builder is its only member. ([#11572](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/pull/11572))
    - Lists and runs agents, teams, and workflows, and reads platform activity and schedules.
    - Uses Company, docs, source-file, and custom OS Manager tools, and reads the current chat history.
    - Its context includes accessible components, and every tool keeps its own permission check.
- **Company OS:** Routines get a dedicated runner, Tasks carry richer state, and published Studio components can execute work.
    - **Mini Agent for Routines:** Routines run on a restricted, non-chat Mini Agent with Company tools and packaged Routine skills, but no platform or general run tools. It is hidden from agent discovery, MCP, and A2A, and refuses non-Routine runs. ([#11572](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/pull/11572))
    - **Task coordination:** Tasks expose `last_run` and API-computed `allowed_transitions`, s

title: browser-use/browser-use 1.0.6 — browser-use 1.0.6
body:
`pip install 'browser-use==1.0.6'`

- **BU 4.0 is the default model.** `Agent(task)` and `ChatBrowserUse()` now run `bu-4.0` on the Browser Use gateway instead of `bu-fast`. Pass `llm='bu-4.0-mini'` for simple tasks at the lowest cost, or `llm='bu-4.0-pro'` for the hardest tasks (#6430).
- **This costs more if you pass no `llm`.** BU 4.0 tokens cost 15 times as much as `bu-fast` ($1.80 / $9.00 per 1M input / output tokens, against $0.12 / $0.60), and it runs at high instead of medium reasoning in the default mode. A short test task cost $0.022 instead of $0.0014. To keep the previous model and price, pass `llm='bu-fast'`. Prices: https://docs.browser-use.com/open-source/models
- The first run without a key opens Browser Use login and continues after approval; cloud browsers print their live-view link (#6425).
- Judge gotchas stay grounded in what the run observed (#6418).

PRs: https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use/pull/6430, https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use/pull/6425, https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use/pull/6418, https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use/pull/6431

title: modelcontextprotocol/servers v2.4.0 — v2.4.0
body:
## Security fixes

v2.4.0 fixes six vulnerabilities in three servers. Upgrade `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` to 2.3.0,
and `mcp-server-git` and `mcp-server-fetch` to 2026.11.11.

| Package | Affected | Fixed in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` | all versions before 2.3.0, and date versions 2025.1.14 through 2026.8.31 | 2.3.0 |
| `mcp-server-git` | through 2026.11.4 | 2026.11.11 |
| `mcp-server-fetch` | through 2026.11.4 | 2026.11.11 |

### `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` 2.3.0

* **Reads stay with the file that was checked** (Linux and macOS). The read tools and file resources now open a file relative to the directory that was checked, as writes already did, so a directory swapped for a symlink between the access check and the read can no longer return a file from outside the allowed directories. A FIFO, socket or device is refused rather than read. **On Windows this narrows the race without closing it**, as for writes (#5260) ([GHSA-p9cv-8g75-4xcg](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-p9cv-8g75-4xcg))
* **`move_file` moves only the source it checked.** A move within one device first takes the source out of its own checked directory under a fresh name, so a source directory swapped for a symlink can no longer bring an outside file into the allowed directories, where it would become readable ([GHSA-7m4x-rv66-mxhh](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-7m4x-rv66-mxhh))

### `mcp-server-git` 2026.11.11

* **A repository's own Git configuration can no longer make the server run a program.** A read-only call such as `git_status` on an untrusted repository used to run a command named in its `.git/config` (`core.fsmonitor`, `diff.external`, hooks, filter and merge drivers, signing) with the server's privileges. Every Git command now overrides those settings, and a Git older than 2.31, which would ignore the overrides, is refused ([GHSA-6hqx-gqrx-c5r2](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-6hqx-gqrx-c5r2))
* **`--repository` confinement covers alternate object stores, linked worktrees and links in the Git directory.** A repository inside the allowed one could read another repository's objects through `objects/info/alternates`, or pass a linked worktree's Git directory off as the allowed repository's. Both are refused, as is a symlink in a Git directory that leads outside the allowed repository. **On Windows a directory junction is not yet covered** (#5520) ([GHSA-q74p-4wrc-q7w6](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-q74p-4wrc-q7w6))

### `mcp-server-fetch` 2026.11.11

* **IPv6 site-local addresses are private.** The private-address guard read `fec0::/10` as public. It is now refused, and so is any IPv6 address outside global unicast (`2000::/3`) that does not carry an IPv4 address ([GHSA-3rxj-6jhw-qfv7](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/adv

title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
body: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_α$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.
author: Lihuan Li, Ruiyi Yang, Jiru Wang, Yifan Duan, Xiachong Lin

title: Scaling LLM Agent Tool Access: The MCP Gateway
body: LLM agents increasingly rely on tool calling to complete tasks. Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes tool calling between LLM agents and tool providers. It reduces integration cost and drives rapid growth in tool scale. In production deployments, tool access becomes difficult to scale. On the tool provider side, legacy services are not directly callable through MCP; the rapid protocol development creates ongoing compatibility cost. On the agent side, the number of mounted tools is limited by the LLM context window and inference overhead; mounting a large tool set increases token usage and inference latency and can reduce task success rate. Moreover, for stateful MCP backends with multiple replicas, preserving session affinity increases client-side complexity. We present a cloud-scale MCP Gateway system. It breaks the direct-connect model on the data plane and offloads legacy service integration, consolidating incompatible MCP variants, access control, tool recommendation, and session-aware routing at the gateway. The conversion module supports 315 OpenAPI services in the cloud and integrates MCP transport variants. Session-aware routing decouples the scalability of the gateway layer and the MCP service layer. The hybrid retrieval engine sustains $\sim$98\% Top-15 recall; it scales agent tool access to 3{,}000+ tools with improved tool selection accuracy. We also share the lessons learned from deploying the gateway system in production.

title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination
body: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.

title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
body: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.

title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
body: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.58. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
body: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

title: MULTILOOP: Evolving Multi-Agent Harnesses for Complex Information-Seeking Tasks
body: The performance of LLM-based agents depends not only on the underlying model but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, and orchestration logic around it. Recent works automate harness optimization with coding agents that analyze execution traces, diagnose failures, and edit the harness code; however, those focused on single-agent systems. Multi-agent harnesses are harder to optimize as fixing them requires changing how agents interact in addition to how each behaves. We study whether automated harness optimization can diagnose and repair failures in multi-agent systems through a case study on complex information-seeking tasks from DeepSearchQA [Gupta et al., 2026]. We apply MULTILOOP, a simple optimization loop in which a coding agent iteratively analyzes, evaluates and edits the harness. With only 10 training samples, the evolved harness improves accuracy by 4.6% over the base harness and by 3.2% over the best single-agent system. However, a taxonomy of failure modes before and after optimization shows that the orchestration failures that characterize multi-agent systems largely persist. Our findings motivate harness optimization methods that encourage structural changes to how agents delegate tasks and share information.

title: Building Agentic AI Systems: A Practical Guide to Architectures, Design Patterns, and Implementation
body: Large language models (LLMs) are moving from answering single prompts to working as agents. An agent is a system that plans, calls external tools, observes the results and repeats until it finishes a task. This tutorial is a practical guide to building such systems. It separates fixed workflows from open-ended agents. It then breaks an agent into four parts: the model, the tools, memory and the control loop. Four common design patterns are covered: ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection and orchestrator-workers. A minimal Python implementation of a tool-using agent loop shows how they work in practice. The guide also covers context engineering, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), evaluation with benchmarks such as SWE-bench, and defences against indirect prompt injection. It closes with open problems in reliability, cost and safety. The goal is to give practitioners a short, well-referenced route from first prototype to a production-ready agentic system. The author used an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) to help draft this tutorial and takes full responsibility for its content.
